title: SHE BURIED SEVEN HUSBANDS. THEN JESUS REVEALED SOMETHING ABOUT ETERNITY THAT LEFT HIS ENEMIES SPEECHLESS.
paragraphs: SHE BURIED SEVEN HUSBANDS. THEN JESUS REVEALED SOMETHING ABOUT ETERNITY THAT LEFT HIS ENEMIES SPEECHLESS.

They thought a woman with seven marriages could make the resurrection look ridiculous. But Jesus turned their impossible question into a revelation about death, love, and the God who refuses to abandon His people to the grave.
“Therefore in the resurrection whose wife shall she be of the seven? for they all had her.” — Matthew 22:28 (KJV)
Imagine standing beside a grave.
The earth is still fresh. The mourners have gone home. The prayers have ended. And someone you thought would grow old beside you is no longer there.
Now imagine doing it again.
And again.
Seven times.
Seven husbands. Seven funerals. Seven chapters ending in death.

And then imagine someone taking that story—not to comfort the grieving woman, not to ask whether she is surviving, not even to acknowledge her suffering—but to use her as the centerpiece of an argument against the resurrection.
That is the question they brought to Jesus.
But what happened next was far more than a debate about marriage in heaven.
Jesus was about to expose a terrible mistake people still make today.
They had measured eternity by the limitations of this world.
And before this encounter was over, the very Scriptures they claimed to understand would testify against them.
Because the question was never really about seven husbands.
It was about whether death gets the final word.
And perhaps that is why this ancient conversation matters more to your life than you realize.

Because somewhere between the people you have buried, the relationships you have lost, the prayers that remain unanswered, and the future you cannot control, you have probably asked your own version of the same question.
Lord, what happens after all this?
Will anything I have loved survive?
Is the grave really the end?
Listen carefully to what Jesus said.
It may change how you understand eternity.
And it may change how you live tomorrow.
The scene unfolds in Matthew 22:23–33, during the final week before Jesus' crucifixion.
Religious leaders had been confronting Him with difficult questions, attempting to challenge His authority and discredit His teaching.
Then came the Sadducees.

Unlike the Pharisees, the Sadducees rejected the resurrection of the dead. Matthew explicitly tells us that they said there was no resurrection (Matthew 22:23). Acts 23:8 likewise records their denial of resurrection, angels, and spirits.
To them, the idea of the dead rising again was not merely questionable.
It was something they intended to challenge.
So they approached Jesus with what appeared to be an airtight argument.
They appealed to a law given through Moses.

In Deuteronomy 25:5–10, the law provided that, under specified circumstances, when a married man died without a son, his brother was to marry the widow and preserve the deceased brother's family line.
This was known as levirate marriage, from the Latin word levir, meaning a husband's brother.
The provision addressed family continuity, inheritance, and the vulnerable position of widows within ancient Israelite society.
The Sadducees constructed a hypothetical situation around that law.
A man married a woman and died without children.
His brother married her.
Then he died.
A third brother married her.
He died too.
The pattern continued until all seven brothers had married the same woman, each dying without leaving children.
Finally, the woman herself died.
Then came their question.
“Therefore in the resurrection whose wife shall she be of the seven? for they all had her.” — Matthew 22:28 (KJV)
Can you hear the trap?
If Jesus said she belonged to the first husband, what about the other six?
If He said she belonged to the seventh, what about the first six?
If He said she belonged to all seven, they could portray the resurrection as producing an impossible marital arrangement.
They assumed the world to come would operate under precisely the same conditions as the present world.
And because they could not make those conditions fit their hypothetical scenario, they thought they had exposed a contradiction.
But there was something deeply revealing about their question.
They had constructed an entire argument around a woman's marriages without asking anything about the woman herself.
Her name was not given.
Her feelings were not mentioned.
Her grief was irrelevant to their argument.
She existed in their hypothetical story as a problem to be solved.
And perhaps someone reading this knows what it feels like to be reduced to a problem.
People remember your divorce but forget your tears.
They remember your failure but ignore the years you fought to survive.
They know what happened to your family but never ask what happened inside your heart.
They discuss your circumstances as though your life were a theological puzzle.
Yet you are not a puzzle.
You are a person made in the image of God.
And the Gospel reveals a Savior who sees people beyond the labels others attach to them.

Now, we must be careful with the passage. Matthew does not tell us that this particular woman actually existed. The Sadducees presented a hypothetical case, and Scripture does not describe her emotions or personal history.
But the scenario was built around a reality Jesus' listeners understood.
Death separates people.
And separation hurts.
That is not hypothetical.
That is painfully real.
Then Jesus answered.
Not with embarrassment.
Not with uncertainty.
Not by choosing one of the seven brothers.
He challenged the foundation of their thinking.
“Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of God.” — Matthew 22:29 (KJV)
In the Greek text, Jesus says:
πλανᾶσθε μὴ εἰδότες τὰς γραφὰς μηδὲ τὴν δύναμιν τοῦ θεοῦ.
Planasthe mē eidotes tas graphas mēde tēn dynamin tou theou.
A faithful translation is:
“You are mistaken, because you do not know the Scriptures or the power of God.”
The Greek verb πλανᾶσθε (planasthe) carries the sense of being mistaken, deceived, or led astray.
Jesus identified two failures.
They misunderstood Scripture.
And they underestimated God's power.
Those two mistakes still travel together.
When we misunderstand God's Word, we can begin imagining that His promises must fit inside the limits of our own experience.
And when we underestimate His power, we begin treating our present circumstances as though they define what is possible forever.
We look at a broken marriage and assume love can never be restored.
We look at a buried dream and assume God can never bring purpose out of disappointment.
We look at a grave and assume death has the final word.
But Jesus did not allow the Sadducees to define the resurrection by what they had already experienced.
He revealed that the coming resurrection belongs to an order of existence greater than the present one.
“For in the resurrection they neither marry, nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven.” — Matthew 22:30 (KJV)
Read that again.
Jesus did not say human beings become angels.
He said that, with respect to marriage, resurrected people are like the angels in heaven.
The distinction matters.

Human beings remain human beings in the resurrection. Jesus Himself rose bodily from the dead, and the New Testament teaches the future resurrection of His people (Luke 24:39; 1 Corinthians 15:42–49).
The parallel account in Luke makes the teaching even clearer.
Jesus says that those who are considered worthy to attain the resurrection cannot die anymore, and in that respect are like angels (Luke 20:34–36).
The Greek expression in Luke 20:36 is:
ἰσάγγελοι γάρ εἰσιν
Isangeloi gar eisin.
Meaning:
“For they are equal to angels” or “for they are like angels.”
The context concerns their deathless condition, not a transformation of human beings into angelic creatures.
And this is where the Sadducees' entire argument collapses.
They assumed marriage in the resurrection must function exactly as it does in this present age.
Jesus explained that it does not.
Marriage is a holy and meaningful institution established by God for human life in this world.
But the resurrection is not simply the continuation of this world's arrangements.
It is the transformation of human existence through God's power.
And for some readers, that raises an unexpectedly painful question.
Does that mean I will not love my husband in heaven?
Will I recognize my wife?
Will the years we shared mean nothing?
Will the person I buried become a stranger to me?
Scripture does not answer every detail of those questions.
We should not pretend that it does.

Jesus explicitly teaches that marriage as an earthly covenant does not continue in the resurrection. But He does not teach that redeemed people lose their identities, their capacity for love, or all recognition of one another.
The Bible gives us reason to hope in personal continuity and perfected fellowship with God, while leaving some details of our future relationships unrevealed.
First Corinthians 13:12 points toward a fuller knowledge than we possess now.
Revelation 21:3–4 promises that God will dwell with His people and wipe away every tear.
And Revelation 19:7–9 describes the marriage supper of the Lamb, directing our attention toward the glorious union of Christ and His redeemed people.
Earthly marriage is not the ultimate destination of human love.
Christ is.
The apostle Paul reveals something extraordinary in Ephesians 5:31–32.
After quoting the foundational words about a man and woman becoming one flesh, Paul says:
“This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church.”
Marriage was never meant to replace God.
At its best, it points beyond itself to the covenant faithfulness and sacrificial love of Jesus Christ.
And that means the resurrection does not diminish the glory of what marriage was designed to signify.
It brings God's people into the presence of the One toward whom that sign was pointing.
Consider what that means.
The love of Christ will not be interrupted by death.
His faithfulness will not expire.
His covenant will not be broken.
And His redeemed people will never again stand beside a grave wondering whether death has stolen everything.
Because in the resurrection, death itself will be defeated.
That is why the next part of Jesus' answer is so astonishing.
He could have ended the conversation after explaining that there would be no marriage in the resurrection.
The hypothetical problem had already been answered.
But Jesus went further.
He addressed the very doctrine the Sadducees denied.
And He did it by taking them back to Moses.

“But as touching the resurrection of the dead, have ye not read that which was spoken unto you by God, saying, I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob? God is not the God of the dead, but of the living.” — Matthew 22:31–32 (KJV)
Do not rush past those words.
Jesus was referring to Exodus 3:6, where God spoke to Moses from the burning bush.
Abraham had died centuries earlier.
Isaac had died.
Jacob had died.
Their bodies had returned to the dust.
Yet God identified Himself through His continuing covenant relationship with them.
In the Hebrew text of Exodus 3:6, we read:
אָנֹכִי אֱלֹהֵי אָבִיךָ אֱלֹהֵי אַבְרָהָם אֱלֹהֵי יִצְחָק וֵאלֹהֵי יַעֲקֹב
Anokhi Elohei avikha, Elohei Avraham, Elohei Yitzchaq, ve-Elohei Ya'aqov.
Meaning:
“I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.”
One important detail deserves careful attention.
Biblical Hebrew frequently expresses present-tense statements without an explicit verb equivalent to the English word am.
Therefore, Jesus' argument should not be reduced to an English grammar trick about the word am.
His point is deeper.
The living God remains faithful to His covenant promises, even when His people have passed through physical death.
The patriarchs' deaths had not canceled God's relationship with them.
And the God whose covenant faithfulness extends beyond the grave has the power to raise the dead.
Luke's account reinforces this meaning when Jesus declares:
“For he is not a God of the dead, but of the living: for all live unto him.” — Luke 20:38 (KJV)
The resurrection is not based on human imagination.
It is grounded in the identity, power, and covenant faithfulness of God.
That is what the Sadducees failed to understand.
They thought death had made the promises of God impossible.
Jesus revealed that death cannot make the living God unfaithful.
And there is a difference between those two ways of seeing the world.
A difference large enough to change how a person grieves.
How a person suffers.
How a person hopes.
And how a person faces the end of earthly life.
Perhaps you have buried someone you loved.
Perhaps the hospital room is still vivid in your memory.
The sound of the machines.
The smell of the hallway.
The phone call you were afraid to answer.
The last conversation you keep replaying.
Maybe you still remember the exact moment when you realized that someone who had always been part of your world would no longer walk through the door.
Christian faith does not require you to pretend that such loss is small.
Jesus Himself wept at the tomb of Lazarus (John 11:35).
The Son of God stood in the presence of death and wept.
He did not rebuke Mary and Martha for grieving.
He did not tell them their tears were evidence of weak faith.
He entered their sorrow.
And then He declared:
“I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live.” — John 11:25 (KJV)
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not merely say, I know about the resurrection.
He did not say, I can explain the resurrection.
He said:
“I am the resurrection, and the life.”
Resurrection hope is not merely a doctrine to memorize.
It is inseparable from a Person.
Jesus Christ.
And this is where the story of the seven brothers becomes far more than a religious debate.
Because the One answering questions about the resurrection was Himself walking toward death.
Within days, Jesus would be arrested.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crowned with thorns.
Nailed to a Roman cross.
His enemies would see Him hanging there.
His disciples would scatter.
His body would be laid in a tomb.
And for a moment, it would appear that death had answered every question.
The Teacher was silent.
The miracle worker was buried.
The One who spoke of everlasting life had entered the grave.
But the story was not finished.
On the third day, Jesus Christ rose bodily from the dead.
Not as a metaphor for optimism.
Not merely as a memory preserved by His followers.
The apostles proclaimed that God had raised Him from the dead, and that His resurrection was witnessed by those who encountered Him (Acts 2:24, 32; 1 Corinthians 15:3–8).
Paul wrote:
“But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept.” — 1 Corinthians 15:20 (KJV)
The word firstfruits matters.
In biblical imagery, the firstfruits were the beginning of a harvest.
Christ's resurrection is not presented as an isolated miracle with no consequences for anyone else.
It is the decisive beginning and guarantee of the resurrection hope belonging to those who are His.
The Sadducees asked Jesus how the resurrection could possibly work.
But the Gospel declares something infinitely greater.
The One they questioned would Himself conquer the grave.
And that changes everything.
Because Christianity does not offer the promise that you will never suffer.
It does not promise that every marriage will be healed in this life.
It does not promise that every disease will disappear, every prayer will receive the answer you want, or every person you love will remain beside you until you are ready to let go.
Jesus never sold that illusion.
He told His disciples that in this world they would have tribulation.
But He also said:
“Be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.” — John 16:33 (KJV)
The Christian hope is not that death is imaginary.
It is that death is a defeated enemy.
First Corinthians 15:26 calls death the last enemy that shall be destroyed.
And Revelation 21:4 promises a future in which death, mourning, crying, and pain will be no more.
Not because human beings finally become strong enough to escape mortality.
But because God makes all things new.
And now comes a question more personal than the one the Sadducees asked.
They wanted to know whose wife the woman would be.
But the Gospel confronts us with a question of far greater importance.
To whom does your life belong?
Because you can spend your whole life trying to solve every mystery about heaven and still refuse the Savior who opens the way to eternal life.
You can argue about marriage after the resurrection while neglecting the condition of your own heart before God.
You can know the Greek words.
You can quote the Hebrew.
You can memorize the passage.
And still miss Jesus.
The Sadducees knew enough Scripture to construct a sophisticated challenge.
But Jesus said they did not truly understand the Scriptures or the power of God.
That warning should humble every one of us.
Biblical knowledge is precious.
Sound doctrine matters.
Careful interpretation matters.
But knowledge that never leads us toward reverence, repentance, faith, and obedience can become another way of hiding from God.
You may be able to win an argument about heaven.
But have you surrendered your life to the Lord of heaven?
You may be able to explain resurrection theology.
But have you trusted the risen Christ?
You may know what Jesus said.
But do you belong to Him?
That is not a question intended to humiliate you.
It is an invitation to examine what matters most.
Because the same Jesus who confronted the Sadducees is the Savior who welcomed sinners, forgave the repentant, touched the unclean, and gave His life for the ungodly.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after we became respectable.
Not after we repaired every broken relationship.
Not after we erased our past.
While we were still sinners.
That is grace.
And grace is not permission to remain enslaved to sin.
It is God's undeserved favor that brings us to Christ and transforms how we live.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God trains us to renounce ungodliness and live godly lives.
The Gospel calls us to repentance and faith.
To turn away from sin.
To trust the crucified and risen Savior.
To receive forgiveness through Him.
And to follow Him in the new life He gives.
Perhaps your scandal was public.
Everyone knew what happened.
Perhaps it was private.
Only you and God know the truth.
Perhaps it was betrayal, addiction, pride, sexual sin, dishonesty, resentment, spiritual compromise, or years of pretending you were closer to God than you really were.
Or perhaps your deepest wound came from what someone else did to you.
The Gospel does not tell us that every wound is our fault.
Nor does it treat every tragedy as punishment for personal sin.
Jesus Himself rejected that simplistic way of thinking in John 9:1–3.
But whether you are carrying guilt that needs repentance or grief that needs comfort, Christ is the One to whom you can come.
He does not ask you to manufacture your own resurrection.
He calls you to trust Him.
From scandal to grace is not the story of sinners becoming impressive enough to save themselves. It is the story of Jesus Christ redeeming people who could never rescue themselves.
And that is why our message at Gospel Warrior is not simply about surviving difficult seasons.
It is about knowing the Savior who entered our broken world, bore sin upon the cross, rose from the grave, and calls us into a transformed life.
There are people reading Christian content every day who are quietly starving for the Word of God.
They attend church but feel afraid to confess their struggles.
They carry Bibles they barely understand.
They hear about grace but have never been discipled in how to walk faithfully with Jesus.
Some have been hurt by religious hypocrisy.
Some have grown cold.
Some have never truly understood the Gospel.
And some are one honest conversation away from admitting that they desperately need help.
This is why we continue creating Scripture-centered messages, Christian resources, devotionals, and discipleship materials.
Not because a Facebook page can save anyone.
It cannot.
Only Jesus Christ saves.
But the Word of God deserves to be faithfully proclaimed, and people need encouragement to open their Bibles, understand the truth, and follow Christ.
These resources are meant to help people study Scripture, strengthen their understanding, and develop a more faithful walk with the Lord.
And if this ministry has helped you, we invite you to become part of sustaining and expanding that work.
For those who wish to give from a heart of worship, such support can be part of their Christian generosity and stewardship.
Scripture teaches believers to give willingly, not under pressure.
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
You do not need to purchase access to God's grace.
And your standing before Jesus is never determined by a monthly payment.
But if you believe this ministry is helping people encounter Scripture and grow in Christ, your voluntary support can help us continue and expand that mission.
These are expressions of our appreciation, not the reason anyone should give.
The greater purpose is discipleship.
The greater mission is the Gospel.
And the greatest glory belongs to Jesus Christ alone.
You can still make a meaningful difference.
Not merely to increase a number.
You may not know who that person is.
But God does.
A simple share can place Scripture before someone who might never have searched for it.
You do not have to explain everything publicly.
You do not have to reveal a painful history to prove that you are sincere.
Sometimes a few honest words are enough to begin a conversation in which another believer can encourage you.
And perhaps someone else reading those comments will realize they are not the only one struggling.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, and even those who do not yet believe in Jesus to follow along and examine what the Bible truly says.
Not every question will be answered in one article.
Not every struggle will disappear after one prayer.
But there is great value in returning again and again to the Word of God, learning to understand it faithfully, and allowing its truth to shape the way we live.
And now, before you leave, return to that woman in the Sadducees' question.
Seven husbands.
Seven deaths.
One final question.
“Whose wife shall she be?”
They expected Jesus to become trapped in the complications of earthly relationships.
Instead, He revealed the power of the living God.
They focused on the arrangements of marriage.
Jesus spoke of the resurrection.
They imagined a problem too complicated for eternity.
Jesus revealed that eternity is not limited by the conditions of this dying world.
And the crowds were astonished at His teaching (Matthew 22:33).
But we have an advantage those crowds did not yet possess.
We know what happened after that conversation.
We know about the cross.
We know about the empty tomb.
We know the apostolic proclamation that Jesus Christ has risen.
And because He lives, those who belong to Him have a hope that reaches beyond the cemetery.
This does not mean every human being automatically receives eternal life with Christ regardless of faith. Scripture calls people to repentance and trust in Him (John 3:16–18; Acts 17:30–31).
It means the promise of eternal life is real because the Savior who makes that promise is alive.
So if you are grieving, bring your grief to Jesus.
If you are afraid, bring your fear to Jesus.
If you are trapped in sin, repent and turn to Jesus.
If you have been trusting your own goodness to save you, stop leaning on what cannot bear the weight of eternity.
Trust the crucified and risen Lord.
He is not merely an answer to a religious question.
He is the Savior of sinners.
The conqueror of death.
The resurrection and the life.
And one day, every person will stand before God.
The most important question will not be how many relationships you had, how many people admired you, how much money you possessed, or how convincing your religious arguments sounded.
The question that must confront us now is whether we have received the salvation offered through Jesus Christ.
Because death is real.
Judgment is real.
Grace is real.
And the resurrection of Jesus Christ changes what is possible beyond the grave.
The Sadducees brought Jesus a story in which everyone died.
Jesus answered with the God who gives life.
And that is the unforgettable difference between human reasoning left to itself and the glorious hope of the Gospel.
They asked who would claim the woman after seven graves. Jesus revealed the God whose promises cannot be buried in even one.
